title: 60% win rate over 535 trades and it still lost money, because the average loss was 1.5x the average win
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every week somebody posts a bot here with a **70% win rate** and a green curve, and theres no way to tell if its any good because the number that decides it isnt in the screenshot.

The cleanest example I have is the Powell 10am setup, which was all over my feed, so I had [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) write it as fixed rules and run it on 1m NQ from july 2023 to feb 2026, 1 contract on a 100k account. 535 trades, **60.2% winners**, net -$3,675, profit factor 0.98.

The reason is the size of the losers. Average win $522, average loss $806. At a 60% hit rate the winners need to be about 0.66x the losers just to break even and this came in at 0.65, so it wins most days and bleeds slowly anyway, and a screenshot from one of its good uptrend months would have looked great.

So when a bot gets posted the only things I look for are **average win, average loss and trade count**. Win rate times average win minus loss rate times average loss is your expected value per trade, and under roughly a hundred trades even that is too thin to lean on. On this one it works out to about negative 7 bucks a trade across two and a half years.

comments.author: directheated
comments.body: It's because 95% of this sub is trying to sell their code to some sucker

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: tbh thats exactly why the 70% win rate posts never show the **average loss** beside it. Put the two next to each other and most of them look like this one did.

comments.author: Wonderful-Win2245
comments.body: Why not set a tight SL?

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: A tighter stop shrinks the average loss but it gets tagged more often, so the win rate comes down with it. The lopsided part here is that the stop is measured off the 10am level while the fill comes on the close back through it, so by the time youre in the stop is **already further away than the target**. Id test moving the entry closer to the level before touching the stop.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Fully agree, win rate on its own says very little. Average win, average loss and trade count tell you much more, and the break-even win rate falls out of them in one line. I'd add one more check, which is to split the results by period, because a slow bleed like that can hide behind a few good months. Cymetica's Backtest Labs shows a result with fees included and can hold out the last part of the history, which helps with that.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: yea the period split is the one id add too. on that run the 280 trades in volatile conditions lost $6,764 at a 0.93 profit factor, and the only regime that made money was uptrends, so most of the **"edge"** was just the nasdaq going up.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's a good find, and it's a better result than a smooth curve would have been. When the only profit comes from uptrends, the first thing to compare against is simply holding the index over the same period. If the strategy doesn't beat that, it's mostly market exposure, and then the useful question is whether a filter can turn it off in volatile stretches without fitting the past.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Yea thats the comparison that settles it. Holding the Nasdaq over the same window took 100k to about 170k and this finished at **-3.7%**, so it didnt even keep the exposure it was riding.

280 of the 535 trades landed in volatile conditions and those lost $6,764, so a filter there is the obvious thing to test, and the catch is exactly what you said about fitting it to the past.
